name_ar: أبو زكريا يحيى بن شرف النووي
name_en: Abu Zakariyya Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi
summary: Imam al-Nawawi (631–676 AH) was a Syrian Shafi'i jurist and hadith scholar whose output in forty-four years of life was so prolific and authoritative that he effectively became the definitive voice of the later Shafi'i school. His Riyad al-Saliheen, Forty Hadith (al-Arba'in al-Nawawiyyah), Sharh Sahih Muslim, and al-Majmu' are among the most widely read and taught works in the Islamic world. (Al-Nawawi's Ash'ari aqeedah is part of the accepted Ahl us-Sunnah tradition — see the site's theological guidelines.)
biography:
Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi was born in 631 AH (1233 CE) in Nawa, a town in the Hawran region south of Damascus, from which his nisba (al-Nawawi) derives. His family was respectable but not wealthy, and his father recognized early that his son was unusually gifted. He sent him to study in Nawa, and by the age of nineteen Yahya had arrived in Damascus — which was then at the height of its intellectual and institutional life under the Ayyubid and early Mamluk dynasties — to study at the Dar al-Hadith al-Ashrafiyyah and the Rawahiyyah madrasa.

Al-Nawawi's years in Damascus were marked by an intensity of study that became legendary. His biographers report that he studied from twelve to fifteen different lessons daily and maintained detailed notes on all of them simultaneously. He slept very little, ate sparingly, and dressed simply throughout his life. His zuhd (asceticism) was genuine rather than performed: he is reported to have lived on dried figs and barely cooked bread for years, turning down gifts from wealthy patrons and avoiding any attachment to comfort or social position. These reports are attested by multiple contemporaries and preserved in al-Subki's Tabaqat al-Shafi'iyyah al-Kubra. (al-Subki, Tabaqat al-Shafi'iyyah al-Kubra, Vol. 8)

His principal teacher in fiqh was Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim al-Fazari (known as al-Firkah), who held the chair of the Rawahiyyah madrasa. In hadith his primary teachers were Zayn al-Din ibn Abd al-Da'im and Ibrahim ibn Isa al-Muradi. Al-Nawawi eventually succeeded al-Fazari as the head of the Rawahiyyah madrasa, a position he held until shortly before his death.

Despite dying at forty-four or forty-five years of age, al-Nawawi produced an extraordinary body of work. In Shafi'i fiqh, his al-Majmu' Sharh al-Muhadhdhab is an encyclopedic commentary on the foundational fiqh text of al-Shirazi, running to twenty-three volumes in modern editions (though al-Nawawi completed only the first nine before his death; later scholars completed it). His Minhaj al-Talibin became the standard textbook of Shafi'i fiqh in the later tradition and spawned hundreds of commentaries and supercommentaries. His Rawdat al-Talibin is an abridgment of al-Rafi'i's Sharh al-Wajiz on Shafi'i fiqh in twelve volumes. These three works together defined the trajectory of Shafi'i fiqh for subsequent centuries.

In hadith, his Sharh Sahih Muslim (eighteen volumes in some editions) is the most widely used commentary on Sahih Muslim and integrates Arabic linguistic analysis, Shafi'i legal derivations, and discussion of hadith science. His Riyadh al-Saliheen (Gardens of the Righteous) — a thematic collection of Quranic verses and authentic hadiths on the ethics of daily life — has arguably been the single most read hadith compilation in the Islamic world for seven centuries, used by ordinary Muslims, scholars, and students alike. His al-Arba'in al-Nawawiyyah (Forty Hadith) is the most famous hadith collection for introductory students and remains a standard text in Islamic educational curricula worldwide.

His Tahdhib al-Asma' wa al-Lughat (Correction of Names and Languages) is a biographical dictionary of persons mentioned in hadith and Quranic commentary, useful for disambiguating the enormous number of individuals with similar names in the classical corpus.

In aqeedah, al-Nawawi was an Ash'ari — the dominant school of rational theology among Shafi'i scholars of his period. He accepted the standard Ash'ari interpretive framework for the divine attributes. His brief treatment of aqeedah in the Forty Hadith and in Sharh Sahih Muslim follows this approach. He was not an Athari and should not be read as one; readers from an Athari background will find his approach to certain aqeedah questions different from Ibn Taymiyyah's.

Al-Nawawi returned to Nawa briefly before his death, apparently to care for his father in old age. He died there in Rajab 676 AH (1277 CE). The shortness of his life and the magnitude of his output prompted later scholars to count him among the mujaddidun (renewers) of the Islamic tradition.
